title: How membrane lipids mediate ciliary signaling
text:
The primary cilium is capable of complex and dynamic signal transduction mediated by unique localization and
concentration of molecules, peptides, and lipids within the ciliary compartment. We adapt and develop a novel
tool to decipher the role of phosphatidylserine, a low abundance negatively charged membrane phospholipid
that is enriched at the primary cilium, in ciliary Polycystin signaling. Further clarifying the membrane lipid
environment at the primary cilium will strengthen our understanding of the basic biology of ciliary signal
transduction and focus therapeutic avenues for treatment of diseases of ciliary origin.

title: Developmental Biology Training Program
text:
Our long-standing predoctoral Developmental Biology Training Program prepares creative and rigorous scientific
leaders. Development biology research reveals mechanisms causing congenital defects and adult diseases,
including cancer that originates from uncontrolled developmental programs, and supports innovative tissue
engineering and regenerative medicine. Therefore, the rational design of innovative diagnostics and therapeutics
depends on multifaceted training of the next generation of developmental biologists.

title: Proteomics
text: While cancer initiation is often based on genomic mutations, it is the aberrant signaling networks, defined at the protein level, that bestow a competitive advantage to tumors. From a functional perspective, cancers are fundamentally determined by their proteomes. The signaling networks and biochemical capacities of tumors are controlled at the protein level by posttranslational modifications (PTMs), such as phosphorylation, that can only be evaluated by direct analysis of the proteins involved. The central importance of proteins in cancer is clearly recognizable in our approaches to therapy, as key proteins in signaling pathways are the major targets for targeted pharmacotherapy. Modern proteomic and metabolomics analyses are based on mass spectrometry capabilities that while still improving, have already developed to the point that they are foundational technologies in cancer research and therapy. Both global analysis, that can quantify thousands of proteins, and targeted approaches that provide focused analysis of a limited protein set or of specific PTMs, have become powerful tools in cancer research. Applications of proteomic mass spectrometry in the field of oncology contribute to better comprehension of pathophysiology, and have potential for early diagnosis and the promise of directed therapies. The Proteomics Core contributes to the research programs of KCI members by providing the equipment and expertise necessary for analysis of cellular protein composition and of protein interactions with other molecules. Our goal is to provide expert scientific consultation, technical expertise and access to state-of-the-art mass spectrometry and molecular interaction technologies. Established in 2002, the services provided by the Proteomics Core have contributed to 29 peer reviewed publications during the current grant period, resulting in a 81% increase over the previous submission. Core personnel maintain the instrumentation and software necessary for these specialized analyses, and are a resource for consultation and proteome-specific informatics. The Core focuses primarily on mass spectrometry-based technologies that utilize state-of-the-art accurate mass LC-MS/MS instruments. The Core has three major MS platforms, each of which is equipped for nanospray Ultra High Pressure Liquid Chromatography (UHPLC). These are the Orbitrap Fusion, the Q Exactive Orbitrap and a TSQ Vantage triple quad. This Core represents a convergence of technical capabilities and intellectual expertise assembled to meet the needs of KCI investigators. Molecular interactions are key to understanding protein function and, to address the need for molecular interaction measurements, the Proteomics Core supports Surface Plasmon Resonance (SPR) and Biolayer Interferometry (BLI) instruments. Future advances in intracellular signaling research and the mechanistic determination of cellular transformation and biomarker discovery are facilitated by our ability to direct questions at the protein level and generate quantitative data answering those questions.

title: DROIDp – Drug Research Organoid-Integrated Development Platform: a Combinatorial NAM for Assessment of in vitro Learning and Memory in Drug and Chemical Testing
text: DROIDp integrates human-derived 3D cell systems, sensors, and AI analytics to model neural functions in a human-centered context. It will provide a human-relevant alternative to animal behavior studies, advancing neuroscience and drug screening while enhancing efficiency and ethical standards in preclinical testing.

title: Forecasting emotional disorder symptoms: A dynamical systems and time-series machine learning approach
text:
Emotional disorders are among the primary causes of disability and impairment worldwide, but predicting their
course, which can be used to improve disease management and to deliver more timely and individually tailored
treatment, is notoriously difficult. We propose to create a precision-medicine framework for predicting emotional
disorder symptoms that leverages theoretically relevant time-series measures using modern “forecasting”
machine learning methods. By promoting more accurate predictions of future symptom changes and just-in-time
interventions for emotional disorders, this framework will provide a foundation for alleviating one of the major
causes of disease and financial burden worldwide.

title: A novel, clinically expedient, AAV-based gene therapy for bone healing
text:
This project investigates a new way to heal bone by gene therapy. Genetic material that promotes bone growth
will be introduced into a gap in a rat thigh bone to see whether the gap fills in with new bone. Various laboratory
tests will be performed to determine the quality of the healed bone and to tell us more about the biological
mechanisms responsible for bone formation.

title: Proteomics and Cognitive Decline Following Intracerebral Hemorrhage
text:
Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) results from rupture of a parenchymal arteriole within the brain
and is the stroke subtype with the highest rates of morbidity and mortality. Progressive cognitive
decline is frequent sequalae of ICH, and while risk factors (age, education level, cerebral white
matter disease, ICH size, and ICH location) for post-ICH cognitive decline there are few blood-
based biomarker candidates or therapeutic targets for post-ICH cognitive decline. This proposal
utilizes unbiased proteomics to identify plasma protein, intracellular immune cell proteins, and
immune cell surface proteins at the time of ICH associated with post-ICH cognitive decline.

title: Amygdala Circuits Mediate Adolescent Alcohol Exposure Effects on Pain
text:
Adolescence alcohol use leads to long-term neural and behavioral changes, and it is known that chronic
adolescent alcohol use is associated with hyperalgesia that persists into adulthood. The current proposal will
seek to exam the neurobiological mechanisms and neuropathologies underlying persistent long-lasting
hyperalgesia in adults with a history of adolescent alcohol exposure. Specifically, the studies proposed will utilize
immunohistochemistry, behavioral assessments of pain sensitivity, slice electrophysiology, along with
chemogenetic and optogenetic approaches to examine the effects of adolescent alcohol exposure on long-term
nociception and synaptic transmission of glutamatergic projections from the BLA to vlPAG-projecting CeM cells.

title: Novel intrinsic endothelial stem cells responsible for lung endothelial regeneration and vascular repair in ARDS
text:
Sepsis-induced acute lung injury (ALI) and acute respiratory distress syndrome remains
an intractable disease with a mortality rate as high as 40%. ALI/ARDS bears the hallmark
of inflammatory infiltration and protein-rich edema fluid due to severe disruption of lung
vascular endothelial barrier. The central objective of the proposed studies is to delineate
the cellular mechanisms of endothelial regeneration and vascular repair, and thereby
provide novel therapeutic strategy targeting the intrinsic regenerative and reparative
mechanisms for resolution of inflammatory lung injury to prevent and treat ALI/ARDS.

title: Targeting mechanisms of chromatin plasticity to improve the efficacy of epigenetic solid tumor therapy
text:
DNA methyltransferase (DNMT) inhibitors offer promise for reversing the abnormal DNA methylation patterns in
cancer and for enhancing cancer immunotherapy, yet their efficacy as single agents in solid tumors remains
limited. In the F99 Phase of this proposal, I will target compensatory chromatin plasticity induced by DNMT
inhibitor therapy - specifically the crosstalk between UHRF1-dependent H3K18ub and SUV39H1/H2-mediated
H3K9me3 - to sensitize colon cancer to both DNMT inhibitor and immune checkpoint therapies. In the K00 phase,
I will build on these insights to develop chromatin-targeted approaches that enhance Chimeric Antigen Receptor
(CAR) T cell persistence and function in solid tumors, advancing strategies for more effective solid tumor
immunotherapy.

title: Computational Methods for Assembling Multiple RNA-seq Samples
text:
The new algorithms for assembling multiple RNA-seq samples we have proposed here will improve identifying
novel transcripts and annotating gene structures. Together with existing large-scale RNA-seq data in various
repositories, our multiple-sample assembly methods can therefore be used to construct accurate data-driven
transcriptomes, a prerequisite for downstream expression quantification and differential analysis. As RNA-seq
has become routine assay to measure gene activities, such improvement will therefore widely advance biological
and biomedical research.

title: Quantitative systems biology of glioblastoma cells and their interactions with the neuronal and immunological milieu
text:
Glioblastoma is a deadly primary brain tumor, and there has been almost no progress in developing effective
therapies for this disease over the past 2 decades. The MIT/DFCI Center for Systems Biology of Glioblastoma
will use sophisticated techniques to better understand how growth of these tumors specifically within the brain
affects treatment response and to use this knowledge to develop more effective therapies for this deadly
disease.

title: SCH: Transfer Regression to Enable Cross-Domain Cardiovascular Event Prediction
text: SCH: Transfer Regression to Enable Cross-Domain Cardiovascular Event Prediction This project proposes fundamental novelties (e.g., transfer volume regression) in computer science, data science, and biomedical engineering to address the critical health challenge of lacking a standardized clinical risk prediction for major cardiovascular events (CVe)—defined as stroke, heart attack, heart failure (HF), and death. Our proposal includes a pioneering transfer regression learning method, combined with several novel machine learning and data science techniques, to develop the first smart, standardized, fairness-aware, and user-friendly CVe prediction model. This model leverages commonly used, low-cost (sometimes free), safe, and quick screening programs (featuring low radiation and no need for contrast agents), aiming to significantly enhance clinical outcomes. The efficacy and robustness of this model are to be validated using four large and diverse datasets, exemplifying a significant advancement in Smart Health and Biomedical Research in the era of Artificial Intelligence and Advanced Data Science (SCH). RELEVANCE (See instructions): We will develop and validate transfer volume regression to enable quantitative clinical risk predictions for major cardiovascular events (defined as stroke, heart attack, heart failure, and death in this proposal) to guide preventive therapy.

title: Novel Therapeutic Approaches for NPC Disease
text:
The enclosed project aims to develop new therapeutic approaches for the fatal disorder, Niemann-Pick Type
C. We will investigate the role of endogenous peptides as modulators of a newly identified receptor that can
regulate cholesterol level as a means to develop treatments for this devastating disease.

title: Quantifying cardiometabolic risks by AI based assay of photoplethysmogram data
text:
Project Narrative / Relevance to public health
Cardiometabolic diseases (CMDs) are major causes of morbidity and mortality worldwide in the face of the
escalation of obesity in populations of mid-to-high income countries despite the significant progress in
prevention and treatment of cardiovascular diseases (CVDs). The proposed research will develop a
standardized approach for performing noninvasive acquisition of photoplethysmogram (PPG) data from two
sites of index finger in a human subject study of 250 participants for extraction of high-quality blood
pressure wave (BPW) waveform signals. The proposed research will also establish and validate an artificial
intelligence (AI) based platform method to obtain an effective panel of CMD biomarkers from the BPW
waveform signals from the study participants by integration of three modeling tools with deep neural
networks.

title: The interface of transcription, DNA damage and epigenetics: A therapeutic vulnerability of the EWS-FLI1 transcription factor
text:
We have developed and clinically translated the combination of trabectedin and irinotecan as an EWS-FLI1
targeted therapy for Ewing sarcoma. While the clinical evaluation of this combination is promising and
multiple tumor regressions have been observed, the activity has been limited by what appears to be intrinsic
mechanisms of resistance. The goal of the current study is to exploit these mechanisms to develop novel
EWS-FLI1 directed combination therapies with improved activity and less toxicity.

title: OCT imaging of the human inner ear
text:
Diseases of the inner ear lead cause patients to experience hearing loss and dizziness, but unfortunately, we
have no effective way to guide the treatment of these disorders because current clinical techniques cannot
image the delicate tissues within the inner ear that underlie these problems. Here we will validate the use of
optical coherence tomography, a safe high-resolution imaging technique that uses low-power light, to see
inside the human inner ear in normal controls, in subjects with Meniere’s disease, and subjects with vestibular
schwannoma. This exciting technology may provide a better approach to diagnosing the cause of hearing loss
and dizziness in individual patients, as well as provide a better way to monitor the effectiveness of treatment.

title: Identifying and characterizing a stimulatory immune checkpoint in macrophage immunosurveillance
text:
Tumor-associated macrophages are key components of the tumor microenvironment. The anticancer functions
of macrophages are tightly regulated through interactions between immune checkpoints and corresponding
receptors. This study seeks to identify and characterize a stimulatory immune checkpoint involved in
macrophage-mediated immunosurveillance, elucidating the fundamental mechanisms underlying cancer-
immune interactions.

title: Developing tools to study HPV16 in oropharyngeal tissues
text:
Project Narra+ve
HPVs, notably HPV16, contribute to 5% of global cancer cases, with HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancers
surpassing cervical cancers in the US. We aim to develop molecular tools to study HPV16-driven oropharyngeal
cancer, addressing challenges in generaDng primary cells with episomal viral DNA, and quanDfying lifecycle
stages and tumorigenicity across HPV16 variants, vital for advancing research and understanding HPV's role in
oropharyngeal cancers.

title: Cell and Screening Core
text: Core B. Cell and Screening Core Summary The focus of the Cell and Screening Core (Core B) is to provide the Projects with cells from diverse mammal species, validated virus stocks, and high throughput screening of virus infections across the “fibroblast zoo” with and without immune perturbation and plasmid and siRNA tools to evaluate virus-host interactions. Viruses need to use host factors to enter cells and complete their replication cycle and need to evaluate antiviral sensing, signaling, and effector protein responses. Given the complexity of these interactions and the potential involvement of many genes and gene networks live cells are needed to fully define mechanisms of species susceptibility and resistance. Fibroblasts are a relevant cell type to achieve these goals because they are target of early infection with alpha and flavivirus and are involved in sensing infection and serve as a source of virus amplification and the site of infection. Fibroblasts are also an ideal cell type for mechanistic studies because they are easy to grow up in large numbers and manipulate in culture and can also be differentiated into other tissue and cell types. This core includes a research team with diverse expertise in virology (Langlois and Cherry), high throughput screening (Cherry), work with primary cells from diverse species (Langlois, Korody, and Maidelaire), and generating stem cells from non-model animals (Korody). Aim 1 will generate primary dermal fibroblasts from diverse mammals for use in the projects and cores. It will also perform validation studies and measuring sources of biological variation. This core will also dedifferentiate fibroblasts from select species into inducible pluripotent stem cells to then differentiate into other cell types for confirmatory studies within the projects. Aim 2 will generate and validate virus stocks for use in the projects and cores. Finally, Aim 3 will perform high throughput screening of alpha and flavivirus infection across the fibroblasts zoo with and without innate immune perturbation or interferon stimulation. Together Core B will provide cells and viruses for the Projects 1 and 2 for mechanistic studies and will provide screening data for Core C and both Projects to further inform mechanisms and to aid in prioritization of virus-host species to evaluate.
